newsitem.title: USA: Fund settles with SEC in oversees stock scheme.
newsitem.headline: Fund settles with SEC in oversees stock scheme.

text.p: The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission said Wednesday it has settled administrative charges against GFL Ultra Fund Ltd, a British Virgin Islands investment company, involving its sales of unregistered securities purchased overseas.
Without admitting or denying the agency's allegations, the investment fund agreed to the SEC's cease and desist order.

In its administrative order, the SEC alleged the fund abused the agency's so-called Regulation S rule, first adopted by the agency in 1990, which exempts U.S. corporations from registering certain offshore offerings.

The SEC said the fund between April 1994 and January 1995 misused the special exemption by purchasing Regulation S shares and then short-selling its positions in the United States. The agency said the fund profited from this trading technique because it purchased the shares at a 15 to 20 percent discount to U.S. market prices.
"This strategy resulted in a profit for the fund when the fund unwound its positions," the SEC said.
Under the SEC's rule, those securities must be held for at least 40 days before they can be offered to U.S. investors.

"The fund participated in 90 Regulation S deals involving the common stock of 47 issuers, and it engaged in the short selling strategy with respect to some or all of the Regulations S shares purchased in 62 of these deals," the SEC said.

The agency's settlement with GFL Ultra comes after the SEC earlier this year proposed lengthening its Regulation S waiting period to two years to help put an end to what it considers abuses of the special exemption.
Two years ago, the agency released a statement outlining what it considered misuses of the Regulation S exemption.

SEC Commissioner Steven Wallman dissented in the agency's action against the fund. "By the time the latter two releases were issued, Ultra already had ceased its trading strategy," Wallman said in a statement.
"I do not think it is appropriate to bring an 'after the fact' enforcement case at this time, regardless of the fact that the party is settling," Wallman said.
GFL officials could not be reached for comment.
